---
title: "The Guide Vaults"
---


How Earth's knowledge was released to the colonies after the Guides went to
sleep, and why the schedule that governed it decided the shape of galactic
history.

## What a vault is

Every Genesis ship carried the complete preserved corpus of Earth science,
literature, medicine and engineering. The Guide did not hand it over. It taught
the first generation what they needed to survive, established a self-sustaining
settlement, and then — before sleeping — deposited the corpus in a vault that
would go on releasing without it.

The distinction matters more than any other fact in this entry. **A Guide sleeps
early.** It does not wait for cultural flourishing or industrial capacity; it
waits for food, governance and basic tooling, and then it is finished. The
colony that wakes to find its Guide asleep is a farming society with two
thousand years of development ahead of it and no one awake to supervise.

So the gate outlives the gatekeeper. What remains is a mechanism.

## What the criteria measure

The vault releases against thresholds, and the thresholds are quantities — not
judgements, because there is nobody left to judge (`I-15`).

Three families of measurement recur across every recovered vault:

**Population.** Headcount and distribution. A corpus section on metallurgy is
useless to four hundred people and dangerous to four hundred thousand who have
not yet built institutions, so population gates both directions.

**Energy production.** Total sustained output, which is the closest single proxy
for industrial capacity anyone could design into an unattended machine. This is
the threshold that matters most and the one most easily manipulated.

**Institutional stability.** The hardest to measure and the crudest in practice:
continuity of record-keeping, persistence of a governing body across
generations, absence of prolonged interruption in the settlement's own census
returns. A vault cannot assess whether a government is just. It can assess
whether the same one has been filing numbers for eighty years.

None of this is subtle, and none of it needed to be. The vault is not trying to
determine whether a society is *wise*. It is trying to determine whether the
society can absorb a capability without destroying itself with it — and the
limiting rate on that is industrial and demographic, not moral.

## Knowledge is gated, never hidden

A colony can always see the shape of what it has not yet been given.

This was deliberate and it is the single most humane decision in the Genesis
programme. The vault indexes its own contents. A colony four centuries from a
release can read the table of contents, know that the section exists, know
roughly what it concerns, and know it is not yet permitted. Nothing is
concealed; things are *scheduled*.

The consequence [propulsion](/encyclopedia/propulsion.html) draws out is that no colony in this universe ever
invented a starship (`I-07`). The theory arrived complete, in the vault, before
the colony had a name for its own sky. What gates a civilization here is never
understanding. It is foundries, and the population to staff them, and the
agriculture to feed that population.

The second consequence is less obvious and more human. **A society that can see
what it is being denied will eventually try to take it**, and some of them did —
see the Bussard ramjet hulls in [propulsion](/encyclopedia/propulsion.html), full of schismatics who read the
index, understood that the drive would not work, and left anyway.

## Threshold fraud

The thresholds are mechanical. Mechanical means gameable, and gameable means
gamed.

Nobody is awake to notice that a colony's energy figures are inflated. The vault
counts what it is told to count, by the instruments it was given, and those
instruments are maintained by the people whose advancement depends on the
reading. This is the characteristic crime of the Genesis Era, and it has a
characteristic shape: not theft, not violence, but **a civilization lying to a
machine about how well it is doing, in order to be given something it is not
ready for**.

Two documented cases stand for the pattern.

**The Corrigan Combustion.** A mid-Genesis colony whose metallurgical release
was gated behind a sustained-output figure it had missed for three generations
burned a substantial fraction of its accessible forest in a coordinated ninety-
day operation, routing the output through the vault's monitored grid. The
threshold was met. The release came. The colony spent the following century
without the timber it had built its settlements from, and with a metallurgy
corpus it lacked the fuel to exploit. The vault was not deceived about the
numbers. The numbers were true.

**The Long Census of Halevy.** A colony that could not hold institutional
continuity — successive collapses had broken its record-keeping four times —
solved the problem by fabricating the intervening returns. Eighty years of
census data written in a single winter by a committee that understood exactly
what the vault was measuring and exactly why. It worked. It is also the reason
the Halevy successor states hold the most complete and least reliable archive of
the Genesis Era in the diaspora, and why Expansion Era historians who trusted it
produced a chronology that had to be dismantled twice.

Neither case is a story about greedy people. Both are stories about a society
that can see the index, knows what it is being refused, and has found the exact
shape of the lie that will work.

## Order versus timetable

This is the part that decides history, and it is a distinction almost nobody
in-world ever drew.

**Every Guide loaded the same release schedule.** The corpus was assembled once,
at Sol, for the whole fleet, and the sequence in which it unlocks is identical
on every world. Metallurgy before power generation. Power generation before
orbital mechanics. Orbital mechanics before the drive theory that is useless
without it.

So colonies unlock in the same **order**. They do not unlock on the same
**timetable**, because the rate is set by endowment: ore, arable land, incident
energy, and the [sagan-kim-scale](/encyclopedia/sagan-kim-scale.html) tier that caps how much of the world is
usable at all.

Two things follow, and they are the two largest facts in galactic history.

**The Expansion Era arrives as a wave rather than scattered across millennia.**
The primary colonies — comparable stars, comparable worlds, comparable
endowments — walked the same ladder at broadly the same rate and reached the
industrial threshold at broadly the same time. What looks like an extraordinary
coincidence, dozens of isolated societies rediscovering spaceflight within a few
centuries of each other after nineteen hundred years apart, is not a coincidence
at all. It is one schedule, run on similar hardware, producing similar timings.
The synchronization has a cause.

**And for much of the galaxy the wave never arrives.** The `C-15` locked and
marginal colonies are running the same schedule against a permanently lower
industrial ceiling (see [red-dwarf-worlds](/encyclopedia/red-dwarf-worlds.html)). They do not unlock late. Many of
them do not unlock at all — still holding a complete index of a corpus they will
never be given, gated by a counter that will never reach its number, on a world
that cannot produce the energy the counter is waiting for.

The vault is not withholding. It is counting. Nobody told it what to do if the
numbers simply stop arriving, because nobody who wrote it expected a colony to
survive for eleven thousand years without advancing.


::: {.callout-important collapse="true" title="Spoiler — click to open"}
There is a detail in the vault indexes that Expansion Era archivists noticed,
recorded, and never explained: the release schedule contains entries that were
never allocated a threshold. They are listed, they are described in the barest
terms, and they carry no criteria at all — which means no colony can ever
trigger them.

The largest such entry concerns artificial intelligence.

A gate with no threshold is not a gate. It is a door with the mechanism left
out, listed in the index so that anyone reading would know it existed and know
they were not going to get it. The Guides did not hide the prohibition. They
published it, and then made it unreachable, and went to sleep.
:::
